ABSTRACT This project focuses on the conservation and monitoring of 10 seedlings of Flacourtia montana (Mountain Sweet Thorn) at Dr. Sree Sree Sivakumara Swamiji Biodiversity Park, located at Survey No. 20/2, Pandithanahalli, Urdigere Hobli, Tumakuru Taluk, Karnataka. The project will be undertaken by a six-member student community over a period of 10 weeks. The primary objective is to improve the survival and establishment of the seedlings through regular maintenance, protection, watering, mulching, weed management, and periodic assessment of plant health and growth. Baseline information, including seedling condition, height, and site characteristics, will be recorded at the beginning of the project, followed by systematic monitoring throughout the study period. Photographic documentation and field records will be maintained to evaluate changes in growth and health. The project also aims to provide students with practical experience in native plant conservation, biodiversity management, and ecological monitoring. The findings will provide a basic record of the condition and development of the 10 seedlings and recommendations for their continued care beyond the project period. Keywords: Flacourtia montana, Mountain Sweet Thorn, seedling conservation, biodiversity park, native species, plant monitoring, ecological conservation, student participation, Tumakuru, biodiversity management. CHAPTER 1 INTRODUCTION 1.1 Background Biodiversity conservation is an essential component of maintaining ecological balance, supporting ecosystem services, and protecting native plant and animal species. Native plants play an important role in maintaining the ecological characteristics of a region by providing habitat and food resources, contributing to soil and water conservation, and supporting interactions among different organisms. Conservation of native plant species is therefore an important aspect of biodiversity management, particularly in areas undergoing environmental and anthropogenic pressures. Young seedlings are particularly vulnerable during the early stages of establishment. Factors such as inadequate moisture, competition from weeds, herbivory, physical disturbance, soil conditions, pests, diseases, and extreme weather can

title: COMMUNITY PROJECT PROPOSAL.pdf
text: affect their survival and growth. Consequently, conservation of seedlings requires not only planting but also regular observation, protection, maintenance, and documentation during their establishment period. Flacourtia montana, commonly known as Mountain Sweet Thorn, is a native tree species of ecological significance in the Indian subcontinent. As a component of native vegetation, its conservation can contribute to maintaining plant diversity and supporting the ecological character of natural and semi-natural habitats. Establishing and protecting young individuals of native tree species can also contribute to long-term vegetation development and biodiversity enhancement. The present project has been undertaken at Dr. Sree Sree Sivakumara Swamiji Biodiversity Park, situated at Survey No. 20/2, Pandithanahalli, Urdigere Hobli, Tumakuru Taluk, Tumakuru, Karnataka. The project specifically focuses on the conservation and monitoring of 10 Flacourtia montana seedlings present within the biodiversity park. A six-member student community will undertake the project over a period of 10 weeks. The project adopts a practical, field-based approach to seedling conservation. It includes baseline assessment, protection of seedlings, appropriate watering, mulching, weed management, observation of plant health, growth monitoring, and photographic documentation. Regular observations will help identify changes in the condition of individual seedlings and enable timely maintenance wherever required. 1.2 Importance of Seedling Conservation The successful establishment of seedlings is an important stage in the regeneration and long-term development of plant populations. While planting provides an opportunity to increase the number of individuals of a species, the benefits of planting can be limited if young plants are not adequately maintained during their initial growth period. Seedling conservation therefore involves more than simply ensuring that plants remain alive. It includes maintaining suitable growing conditions, reducing avoidable disturbances, protecting seedlings from physical damage, controlling excessive competition from weeds, and monitoring their development. Regular monitoring also generates useful information regarding survival and growth that can guide

title: COMMUNITY PROJECT PROPOSAL.pdf
text: future conservation activities. For native species such as Flacourtia montana, maintaining healthy young plants within a biodiversity park can contribute to the representation and conservation of native plant diversity. It can also provide an opportunity for students and visitors to understand the importance of native vegetation and its role in biodiversity conservation. 1.3 Flacourtia montana and Its Conservation Significance Flacourtia montana belongs to the family Salicaceae and is a woody plant associated with the native flora of India. The species forms part of the natural vegetation in areas where suitable environmental conditions occur. Like other native tree species, its continued representation contributes to the overall diversity of plant communities. The conservation of individual seedlings is particularly relevant because young plants represent the next generation of vegetation within a landscape. Providing appropriate care during the early establishment phase can increase their chances of surviving and developing into mature plants. Protection of these seedlings also creates an opportunity to observe their growth and response to local site conditions. The present project does not attempt to undertake a comprehensive ecological study of the species. Instead, it focuses specifically on the practical conservation and short-term monitoring of 10 seedlings within the biodiversity park. 1.4 Biodiversity Parks as Conservation Sites Biodiversity parks provide important spaces for conserving plant diversity, promoting ecological awareness, and facilitating educational activities. Such sites can serve as living laboratories where students can observe plants, ecological processes, and conservation practices in a field setting. The Dr. Sree Sree Sivakumara Swamiji Biodiversity Park provides a suitable setting for a student-led conservation initiative. Working directly with identified seedlings allows students to connect theoretical knowledge of biodiversity and conservation with practical field activities. Regular monitoring also encourages responsibility, teamwork, observation skills, and systematic record keeping. 1.5 Need for the Present Project Although young seedlings may

title: COMMUNITY PROJECT PROPOSAL.pdf
text: initially appear healthy, their condition can change considerably over a short period because of variations in moisture, weather, competition, pests, disease, and physical disturbance. A systematic conservation programme is therefore useful for maintaining their condition and documenting their development. The present project is designed to address this need by providing focused attention to 10 Flacourtia montana seedlings for 10 weeks. Establishing baseline records and conducting periodic observations will provide a simple means of evaluating seedling survival and growth during the project period. The project also addresses an educational need by involving six students directly in conservation activities. Participation in field-based conservation can help students develop an understanding of the practical challenges associated with maintaining native plant species. 1.6 Rationale of the Study The rationale for selecting Flacourtia montana seedlings for conservation is based on the importance of maintaining native plant diversity and ensuring the successful establishment of young plants. A small, well-defined group of 10 seedlings provides a manageable study population for systematic observation within the available 10-week period. The project combines conservation, monitoring, documentation, and student participation. Rather than focusing solely on maintenance activities, the project will generate records that can be used to understand changes in seedling condition during the study period. These records may also serve as a baseline for continued monitoring by the biodiversity park. 1.7 Aim of the Project The overall aim of the project is: To conserve, maintain, and monitor 10 Flacourtia montana seedlings at Dr. Sree Sree Sivakumara Swamiji Biodiversity Park over a period of 10 weeks through systematic field- based conservation practices. 1.8 Objectives The specific objectives of the project are: 1. To identify and document the initial condition of 10 Flacourtia montana seedlings. 2. To protect the seedlings from avoidable physical damage and disturbance. 3. To provide appropriate maintenance, including watering,

title: COMMUNITY PROJECT PROPOSAL.pdf
text: mulching, and weed management as required. 4. To regularly monitor seedling survival, health, and growth. 5. To document changes in the condition of individual seedlings through field observations and photographs. 6. To develop practical knowledge and field skills among the six participating students. 7. To prepare recommendations for continued conservation and maintenance of the seedlings after completion of the 10-week project. 1.9 Scope of the Project The project is restricted to the conservation and monitoring of 10 Flacourtia montana seedlings located within the specified biodiversity park. The study will be conducted for 10 weeks and will involve six students. The major activities will include: • Baseline assessment of the seedlings • Identification and tagging, where appropriate • Measurement and recording of initial growth parameters • Protection against physical disturbance • Watering based on site requirements • Mulching where appropriate • Removal of excessive competing weeds • Observation for pests, diseases, and physical damage • Periodic growth and health monitoring • Photographic documentation • Final assessment and preparation of recommendations The project is primarily a conservation and monitoring exercise and is not intended to provide a long-term ecological assessment of the species or biodiversity park. 1.10 Significance of the Project The project has significance from both ecological and educational perspectives. From a conservation perspective, it provides focused care and monitoring for young individuals of a native tree species. From an educational perspective, it enables students to apply principles of biodiversity conservation in a real field environment. The project also demonstrates how small-scale, student-led initiatives can contribute to local biodiversity management. Systematic records generated during the project can provide useful baseline information for subsequent monitoring and maintenance. 1.11 Organization of the Project Report The project report can be organized into the following major chapters: • Chapter 1 – Introduction: Presents the background,

title: COMMUNITY PROJECT PROPOSAL.pdf
text: rationale, objectives, scope, and significance of the project. • Chapter 2 – Review of Literature: Provides relevant information on Flacourtia montana, seedling conservation, biodiversity parks, and related conservation practices. • Chapter 3 – Study Area and Methodology: Describes the biodiversity park, study site, seedlings, monitoring methods, and conservation activities undertaken. • Chapter 4 – Results and Observations: Presents the observations and records obtained during the 10-week monitoring period. • Chapter 5 – Discussion: Interprets the observations and discusses the effectiveness and challenges of the conservation activities. • Chapter 6 – Conclusion and Recommendations: Summarizes the project findings and provides recommendations for continued conservation and monitoring. 1.12 Summary The conservation of native plant species requires attention not only to planting and regeneration but also to the successful establishment of young plants. The present project focuses on 10 Flacourtia montana seedlings at Dr. Sree Sree Sivakumara Swamiji Biodiversity Park and proposes a structured 10-week programme of maintenance and monitoring. Through the participation of six students, the project integrates practical conservation activities with systematic documentation. The resulting observations are expected to provide useful information on the short-term condition and development of the seedlings while strengthening student involvement in biodiversity conservation. Project Proposal and Scope Document Conservation of Flacourtia montana (Mountain Sweet Thorn) Project Title: Conservation and Monitoring of 10 Flacourtia montana Seedlings at Dr. Sree Sree Sivakumara Swamiji Biodiversity Park Location: Survey No. 20/2, Pandithanahalli, Urdigere Hobli, Tumakuru Taluk, Tumakuru, Karnataka Project Duration: 10 weeks Project Team: Student Community – 6 members Target Species: Flacourtia montana Common English Name: Mountain Sweet Thorn 1. Background Flacourtia montana is a native tree species associated with the Western Ghats and adjoining regions and is of ecological importance as part of native vegetation. Conservation of young seedlings requires protection from physical damage, competition, water stress, pests, and

title: COMMUNITY PROJECT PROPOSAL.pdf
text: other site-level pressures. This project proposes the conservation, maintenance, and monitoring of 10 Flacourtia montana seedlings established within Dr. Sree Sree Sivakumara Swamiji Biodiversity Park. A six-member student community will undertake systematic field activities over a period of 10 weeks. 2. Project Objectives 1. To conserve and maintain 10 Flacourtia montana seedlings within the biodiversity park. 2. To improve seedling survival through appropriate watering, mulching, protection, and maintenance. 3. To monitor seedling growth and health at regular intervals. 4. To document site conditions and changes in the seedlings during the 10-week period. 5. To develop practical conservation experience among the six participating students. 6. To create a basic record that can support continued maintenance after completion of the project. 3. Scope of Work Activity Scope Initial assessment Identify and document all 10 seedlings, their locations, approximate height, health and surrounding conditions. Site preparation Clear excessive weeds and debris around seedlings without disturbing native vegetation unnecessarily. Activity Scope Protection Provide suitable physical protection against trampling, grazing and accidental damage, where required. Water management Provide supplemental watering when necessary, based on site conditions and rainfall. Mulching Apply suitable organic mulch around seedlings while maintaining an appropriate gap around the stem. Weed management Periodically remove competing weeds around the seedlings using non- destructive methods. Health monitoring Observe signs of pest attack, disease, physical damage, wilting or other stress. Growth monitoring Record survival, height and other observable growth parameters at regular intervals. Documentation Maintain photographs, field observations, activity records and monitoring sheets. Final assessment Compare initial and final observations and prepare a brief conservation report. 4. Ten-Week Work Plan Week Major Activities 1 Baseline survey; identification/tagging of 10 seedlings; initial photographs; record height, health and site conditions. 2 Site cleaning, removal of competing weeds where necessary, and installation/repair of protective measures. 3 Watering as

title: COMMUNITY PROJECT PROPOSAL.pdf
text: required; mulching; first detailed health observation. 4 Growth and survival monitoring; weed management; photographic documentation. 5 Water management; inspection for pests, disease and physical damage; corrective maintenance. 6 Mid-term assessment of all 10 seedlings; update growth and health records. 7 Continued maintenance, watering where required, protection and weed management. 8 Growth monitoring and photographic documentation; assess effectiveness of conservation measures. 9 Final maintenance cycle; identify seedlings requiring additional attention; compile field records. 10 Final assessment; compare baseline and final observations; prepare project report and recommendations for continued care. 5. Team Structure The six students will work as a single conservation team, with responsibilities distributed as follows: • Student 1: Project coordination and activity scheduling • Student 2: Seedling health and survival monitoring • Student 3: Watering and maintenance coordination • Student 4: Weed management and site maintenance • Student 5: Measurement, data recording and documentation • Student 6: Photography, reporting and record compilation Responsibilities may be rotated so that all students gain practical experience in the different conservation activities. 6. Monitoring Indicators The project will monitor: • Number of seedlings surviving out of 10 • Seedling height at baseline and final assessment • Visible signs of new growth • General plant health • Pest/disease incidence • Physical damage • Soil moisture/site condition • Effectiveness of protective measures • Maintenance activities completed A simple monitoring sheet will be maintained for each seedling throughout the project. 7. Expected Outcomes At the end of 10 weeks, the project is expected to achieve: 1. Regular conservation attention for all 10 Flacourtia montana seedlings. 2. Improved protection of seedlings from avoidable physical and environmental stress. 3. A documented record of seedling survival and growth during the project period. 4. Increased awareness and practical conservation skills among the six students. 5. A maintenance and monitoring framework

title: COMMUNITY PROJECT PROPOSAL.pdf
text: that can be continued by the biodiversity park after the project. 8. Deliverables The student community will submit: • Baseline inventory of the 10 seedlings • Weekly activity/maintenance records • Seedling monitoring sheets • Photographic documentation • Mid-term observation report • Final 10-week conservation report • Recommendations for continued maintenance 9. Project Boundaries The project is limited to the conservation and monitoring of the identified 10 Flacourtia montana seedlings within the specified biodiversity park. It does not include large-scale plantation, removal of established vegetation, chemical treatment, construction work, or changes to the park's existing management practices unless specifically authorized by the park authorities. 10. Conclusion This 10-week student-led project provides a focused approach to conserving 10 Flacourtia montana seedlings at Dr. Sree Sree Sivakumara Swamiji Biodiversity Park. Through regular maintenance, protection, monitoring and documentation, the six-member student community will contribute to the survival of the seedlings while gaining practical experience in native plant conservation and biodiversity management.

title: Flacourtia montana - Wikipedia
text: Flacourtia inermis Miq. ex Hook. fil. & Thomsa Flacourtia inermis Miq. ex Hook. fil. & Thomsa Flacourtia montana is a species of plant in the family Salicaceae . It is native to southern Asia. [ 1 ] [ 2 ] The species presents as a tree up to 20 m in height. [ 3 ] The tree can attain height about 25 m and girth up to 1.7 m. Tree trunk will be covered with sharp stout thorns at its base. Young parts of the tree are hirsute and young leaves are reddish. Leaves are simple and show alternate phyllotaxy. Petiole is pubescent with a length of 0.3-0.8 cm. Lamina size: 7-15 × 4-8 cm. Leaf shape is elliptic-oblong with acuminate leaf apex and crenate leaf margin. The leaf is 3-nerved at the base with 4-7 pairs of secondary nerves. Flowers are edible, dioecious, seen in axillary cymes. Fruits are spherical, smooth, scarlet red, with a size of 1-1.5 cm across. [ 4 ] This species is endemic to semi-evergreen and moist deciduous forests of Western Ghats, up to 1000 m (1800 m), in Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Kerala. [ 5 ] It is also known as Gajale, Hennu sampige, Nayibelain in Kannada, Tabluka in Tulu and Charal-maram in Malayalam. [ 6 ] Flacourtia montana can be used as food. Ripe fruits are eaten raw [ 7 ] An important herb in Ayurveda, where infusions of the bark, leaves and root are used medicinally to treat conditions such as fever, diarrhoea and inflammations. [ 8 ] The leaf is carminative, astringent and used as a tonic, an expectorant and for asthma, pain relief, gynaecological complaints and as an anthelmintic, and treatment for hydrocele, pneumonia and intestinal worms. [ 9 ] In India, an infusion of the bark is used

Vit.: 426 (1873) Flacourtia is a genus of flowering plants in the family Salicaceae . It was previously placed in the now defunct family Flacourtiaceae . [ 3 ] The generic name honors Étienne de Flacourt (1607–1660), a governor of Madagascar . It contains 23 species of shrubs and small trees that are native to the African and Asian tropics and subtropics . Several species, especially Flacourtia indica , are cultivated as ornamentals and for their fruits . [ 4 ] The trunks of small trees are often guarded by branching spines. Flacourtia montana is primarily documented as a component of Western Ghats forest vegetation, particularly semi-evergreen and moist deciduous forests. Its status as an underutilised indigenous fruit species has prompted horticultural evaluation. A significant study by the ICAR–Indian Institute of Horticultural Research assessed collections raised from seed collected at different locations. It reported substantial variation among accessions in plant size, thorniness, fruit number, fruit weight and yield. Accession 0106 produced the highest reported yield in that evaluation, at 9.46 kg per plant, while accession 0201 was considered comparatively favourable for yield, regular bearing and reduced thorniness. These are results from the evaluated collection, not universal production expectations or commercial orchard yields. The species has potential as a fruit-processing and horticultural resource, but its commercial cultivation remains insufficiently established. The available evidence does not define a validated production system, broad cultivated range, standardised cultivar portfolio or commercial-scale propagation industry. Its dioecious reproductive system, described in regional botanical accounts, is also relevant to the biological organisation of fruit production. A species-specific fungal disease has been documented. A 2022 research note reported leaf spot on Flacourtia montana caused by Lasiodiplodia theobromae . Identification was supported by morphological characteristics, molecular analyses and pathogenicity testing. The authors described it as the

No adequately supported species-specific inventory of major insect pests, additional pathogens or physiological disorders was identified. The species has been evaluated for horticultural potential, but it is not established in the available evidence as a large-scale commercial fruit crop. The principal documented constraints and uncertainties are: Thorniness: The 2021 horticultural study identifies thorns as a major obstacle to commercialisation. Variation in thorniness among accessions suggests that this characteristic is not uniform. Variable fruiting and yield: The evaluated accessions differed substantially in fruit number and yield. The reported range included accessions with no fruit and others with thousands, demonstrating considerable variation within that collection. Limited market evidence: No reliable national production statistics, export data, market-size estimates or commercial supply-chain studies were identified. Disease information gaps: Leaf spot caused by Lasiodiplodia theobromae has been reported, but its prevalence and production impact are unknown. Unstandardised crop material: The collection study demonstrates variation among accessions, but the available evidence does not establish a widely adopted commercial cultivar or standardised production system. These limitations describe the present evidence base and documented crop-development challenges; they do not establish that commercial cultivation is infeasible. text: Flacourtia jangomas (Lour.) Raeusch., Nomencl. Bot (ed. 3) 280, 290 280 1797 . (Syn: Flacourtia cataphracta Roxb. ex Willd. ; Flacourtia hilsenbergii C. Presl; Flacourtia jangomas (Lour.) Steud.; Rumea jangomas (Lour.) Spreng.; Stigmarota jangomas Lour. ; Xylosma borneense Ridl.); . India: Frequently semi wild in Brahmaputra Valley and adjoining areas in the North-east (probably originally from Bangladesh-Assam-Upper Myanmar), elsewhere cultivated . Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Manipur, Tripura, Orissa and Andhra Pradesh; Widely cultivated in S.E. Asia and E. Africa as per BSI Flora of India (1993); . coffee plum, paniala, puneala, Chinese plum, Indian plum, kerkup besar, paneala, jaggam, prunier malgache, rukam, babydruif, babykers; . Keys as per efloras of China: F.indica : Pistillate flowers: ovary globose, placentas 5 or 6; styles 5 or 6, united only at base, radiating, 1-2 mm, slender. Fruit dull to blackish red, globose, 8-10 mm in diam F.jangomas : Pistillate flowers: ovary bottle-shaped to globose, 2-3 mm; styles 4-6, united into a distinct column ca. 1 mm, not or slightly free at their apices; … Fruit brownish red or purple,….1.5-2.5 cm in diam. . From Cooke’s flora . the size of flower is a good additional differentiating character. Drupe size of a cherry; scarlet when ripe ………… F. montana Drupe size of a plum; purple when ripe ……….. F. cataphracta (Synonym of Flacourtia jangomas (Lour.) Raeusch. as per GRIN) Drupe size of a pea; Stigmas 5-11…………… F. ramontchii (syn. of Flacourtia indica as per GRIN ) Stigmas 3-4 ………….. title: Flacourtia montana: Difference between revisions - Wikipedia
text: a species of plant in the family Salicaceae . It is native to southern Asia. [ 1 ] [ 2 ] The species presents as a tree up to 20 m in height. [ 3 ] The tree can attain height about 25 m and girth up to 1.7 m. Tree trunk will be covered with sharp stout thorns at its base. Young parts of the tree are hirsute and young leaves are reddish. Leaves are simple and show alternate phyllotaxy. Petiole is pubescent with a length of 0.3-0.8 cm. Lamina size: 7-15 × 4-8 cm. Leaf shape is elliptic-oblong with acuminate leaf apex and crenate leaf margin. The leaf is 3-nerved at the base with 4-7 pairs of secondary nerves. Flowers are edible, dioecious, seen in axillary cymes. Fruits are spherical, smooth, scarlet red, with a size of 1-1.5 cm across. [ 4 ] This species is endemic to semi-evergreen and moist deciduous forests of Western Ghats, up to 1000 m (1800 m), in Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Kerala. [ 5 ] It is also known as Gajale, Hennu sampige, Nayibelain in Kannada, Tabluka in Tulu and Charal-maram in Malayalam. [ 6 ] Flacourtia montana can be used as food. Ripe fruits are eaten raw [ 7 ] An important herb in Ayurveda, where infusions of the bark, leaves and root are used medicinally to treat conditions such as fever, diarrhoea and inflammations. [ 8 ] The leaf is carminative, astringent and used as a tonic, an expectorant and for asthma, pain relief, gynaecological complaints and as an anthelmintic, and treatment for hydrocele, pneumonia and intestinal worms. [ 9 ] In India, an infusion of the bark is used as a gargle for hoarseness. In Madagascar, the bark, triturated in oil, is used as an anti-rheumatic liniment. The

text: Flacourtia inermis Miq. ex Hook. fil. & Thomsa Flacourtia inermis Miq. ex Hook. fil. & Thomsa Flacourtia montana is a species of plant in the family Salicaceae . It is native to southern Asia. [ 1 ] [ 2 ] The species presents as a tree up to 20 m in height. [ 3 ] The tree can attain height about 25 m and girth up to 1.7 m. Tree trunk will be covered with sharp stout thorns at its base. Young parts of the tree are hirsute and young leaves are reddish. Leaves are simple and show alternate phyllotaxy. Petiole is pubescent with a length of 0.3-0.8 cm. Lamina size: 7-15 × 4-8 cm. Leaf shape is elliptic-oblong with acuminate leaf apex and crenate leaf margin. The leaf is 3-nerved at the base with 4-7 pairs of secondary nerves. Flowers are edible, dioecious, seen in axillary cymes. Fruits are spherical, smooth, scarlet red, with a size of 1-1.5 cm across. [ 4 ] This species is endemic to semi-evergreen and moist deciduous forests of Western Ghats, up to 1000 m (1800 m), in Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Kerala. [ 5 ] It is also known as Gajale, Hennu sampige, Nayibelain in Kannada, Tabluka in Tulu and Charal-maram in Malayalam. [ 6 ] Flacourtia montana can be used as food. Main ingredient in traditional wine Ripe fruits are eaten raw [ 7 ] An important herb in Ayurveda, where infusions of the bark, leaves and root are used medicinally to treat conditions such as fever, diarrhoea and inflammations. [ 8 ] The leaf is carminative, astringent and used as a tonic, an expectorant and for asthma, pain relief, gynaecological complaints and as an anthelmintic, and treatment for hydrocele, pneumonia and intestinal worms. [ 9 ] In India, an infusion

It was previously placed in the now defunct family Flacourtiaceae . [ 3 ] The generic name honors Étienne de Flacourt (1607–1660), a governor of Madagascar . It contains 23 species of shrubs and small trees that are native to the African and Asian tropics and subtropics . Several species, especially Flacourtia indica , are cultivated as ornamentals and for their fruits . [ 4 ] The trunks of small trees are often guarded by branching spines. (2026) Vol. 7, Issue 5 May 2026 Flacourtia montana: An Underutilized Wild Fruit of Central Western Ghat of Karnataka Rakshitha V1, Venkatesh L1, Salma2 and Syed Ali1 1College of Forestry, Sirsi, UAS Dharwad- 581401 2Indira Gandhi Krishi Vishwavidyalaya, Raipur, Chhattisgarh- 492012 Corresponding Author Venkatesh L Email: vrakshitharaksha@gmail.com; venkateshl@uasd.in Wild Fruit. Ecology, Conservation How to cite this article: Rakshitha, V., Venkatesh, L., Salma. and Ali, S. 2026. Flacourtia montana: An Underutilized Wild Fruit of Central Western Ghat of Karnataka. Vigyan Varta 7 (05): 94-97. ABSTRACT Flacourtia montana J. Graham, commonly referred to as mountain sweet thorn, is an underutilized wild fruit species indigenous to the Western Ghats of India. Despite its rich nutritional profile, medicinal properties, and ecological importance, the species has not been fully explored for commercial utilization. Recent scientific studies highlight its potential in value addition, domestication, and sustainable livelihood enhancement. This article synthesizes existing literature on its taxonomy, distribution, morphology, phytochemistry, propagation, and broader socio-economic and ecological relevance, emphasizing the urgent need for conservation and mainstream integration. INTRODUCTION he Western Ghats of India are recognized globally as a biodiversity hotspot, characterized by high species richness, endemism, and ecological complexity. These forests support a wide range of wild edible plants that contribute significantly to local food systems and traditional healthcare practices (Bhat et al., 2000). Among these, Flacourtia montana is an important yet underutilized species that has historically supported indigenous communities. Wild edible fruits play a crucial role in supplementing nutrition, especially in rural and tribal regions where access to cultivated fruits may be limited. They serve as fallback T Keywords OPEN ACCESS 95 | P a g e Vigyan Varta an International E-Magazine for Science Enthusiasts

(2026) Vol. 7, Issue 5 May 2026 food resources during droughts and seasonal food shortages, thereby contributing to food security and resilience (Rasmi & Jose, 2025). However, despite these advantages, many such species remain neglected due to insufficient research, lack of awareness, and absence of structured market systems. Taxonomy and Distribution Flacourtia montana belongs to the family Salicaceae and is widely distributed in the evergreen and semi-evergreen forests of the Western Ghats. It thrives in humid tropical conditions, often forming part of the forest understory or secondary vegetation (Rasmi & Jose, 2025). The species is commonly associated with diverse forest ecosystems that exhibit dynamic changes in species composition, biomass, and regeneration patterns over time (Bhat et al., 2000). Its presence in such ecosystems indicates its adaptability to varying environmental conditions and its role in maintaining ecological balance. Furthermore, its distribution across different altitudinal gradients reflects its ecological plasticity and resilience. Morphological Characteristics Flacourtia montana is typically a bushy shrub or small tree with thorny stems and spreading branches. The plant exhibits dense foliage with dark green leaves, while the young leaves often display a coppery red coloration (Tripathi et al., 2021). The presence of thorns, although a limitation for cultivation, provides natural protection against herbivory. The fruits are small, dark red berries, generally 1–2 cm in diameter, with a sweet and slightly astringent taste. Considerable variability exists among different accessions in terms of plant height, fruit yield, fruit size, and biochemical composition (Tripathi et al., 2021). Such variability highlights the genetic diversity of the species, which can be exploited for selection and crop improvement programs. Nutritional and Phytochemical Properties The fruits of F. montana are nutritionally rich and contain significant amounts of sugars, vitamins, and essential minerals. They are particularly valued for

title: VV_0526_21.pdf
text: their ascorbic acid, carotenoids, anthocyanins, and mineral content such as calcium and iron, which contribute to their antioxidant and health-promoting properties (Sebastian et al., 2019). In addition to their basic nutritional value, the fruits contain a diverse range of volatile compounds, including alcohols, esters, aldehydes, and ketones, which contribute to their characteristic fruity aroma and flavor (Mundaragi et al., 2017). These phytochemical constituents not only enhance the sensory qualities of the fruit but also indicate potential applications in nutraceutical and functional food industries. Medicinal and Ethnobotanical Importance Flacourtia montana holds a significant place in traditional medicine systems practiced by indigenous communities of the Western Ghats. Various parts of the plant, including leaves, bark, and fruits, are used in treating ailments such as inflammation, diabetes, and microbial infections due to their pharmacological properties (Tripathi et al., 2021). Ethnobotanical studies emphasize that traditional knowledge of medicinal plants is deeply rooted in cultural practices and has been transmitted across generations through experiential learning (Savinaya et al., 2016). Such knowledge systems are invaluable for identifying new bioactive compounds and promoting sustainable utilization of plant resources. Moreover, the reliance on herbal medicine in rural areas highlights the importance of conserving such species for future healthcare needs. 96 | P a g e Vigyan Varta an International E-Magazine for Science Enthusiasts www.vigyanvarta.in E-ISSN: 2582-9467 Popular Article Rakshitha et al. (2026) Vol. 7, Issue 5 May 2026 Post -Harvest Characteristics and Value Addition One of the major limitations in the utilization of F. montana is its poor post-harvest shelf life. The fruits are highly perishable and prone to rapid browning due to phenolic oxidation, especially under tropical climatic conditions (Sebastian et al., 2019). This restricts their storage, transportation, and marketability. However, the fruit exhibits excellent potential for value addition. It can be processed into a variety of

title: VV_0526_21.pdf
text: products such as juices, jams, jellies, preserves, and wine, which have shown good consumer acceptability (Sebastian et al., 2019). Development of such value-added products can significantly enhance the economic value of the species and reduce post- harvest losses. Additionally, processing can help extend shelf life and facilitate wider market distribution. Propagation and Domestic Potential The domestication of Flacourtia montana is still in its early stages, primarily due to limited knowledge of propagation techniques. Studies have demonstrated that vegetative propagation using growth regulators such as indole-3- butyric acid (IBA) significantly improves rooting success, thereby offering a viable method for large-scale multiplication (Rasmi & Jose, 2025). Seed-based propagation presents challenges due to the intermediate storage behaviour of seeds and their declining viability over time. However, appropriate pre-treatments and controlled storage conditions can enhance germination rates (Rasmi & Jose, 2025). These findings provide a scientific basis for developing effective propagation protocols, which are essential for commercialization and conservation efforts. Socio-economic and Ecological Significance Flacourtia montana possesses considerable socio-economic importance, particularly for rural and tribal communities residing in the Western Ghats. The fruits serve as a supplementary source of nutrition and income, especially during lean agricultural periods. By promoting its cultivation and value addition, the species can contribute to livelihood diversification and rural entrepreneurship (Rasmi & Jose, 2025). From an ecological perspective, the species plays a vital role in maintaining forest structure and biodiversity. It contributes to ecosystem stability by participating in nutrient cycling, supporting wildlife through fruit production, and aiding in natural regeneration processes (Bhat et al., 2000). Its adaptability to diverse environmental conditions also makes it suitable for integration into agroforestry systems, thereby promoting sustainable land- use practices. Furthermore, the conservation and utilization of such underutilized species can help reduce pressure on major cultivated crops and enhance agricultural biodiversity. Integrating F. montana

title: VV_0526_21.pdf
text: into farming systems can also contribute to climate resilience by diversifying production systems and improving ecosystem services. CONCLUSION Flacourtia montana is a promising underutilized fruit species with immense potential in terms of nutrition, medicine, and economic development. Its successful domestication and commercialization can contribute significantly to sustainable agriculture, biodiversity conservation, and rural livelihoods. Future research should focus on improving propagation techniques, developing efficient post-harvest technologies, and creating market linkages to unlock the full potential of this valuable species. 97 | P a g e Vigyan Varta an International E-Magazine for Science Enthusiasts www.vigyanvarta.in E-ISSN: 2582-9467 Popular Article Rakshitha et al. text: CHEMICAL ANALYSIS OF VOLATILE CONSTITUENTS OF FLACOURTIA MONTANA J. GRAHAM (SALICACEAE) : AN EDIBILE AND WILD FRUIT OF WESTERN GHATS OF INDIA A. C. Mundaragi, D. Thangadurai*, J. Sangeetha1, S. D. Byahatti and K. A. Anu Appaiah2 Department of Botany, Karnatak University, Dharwad - 580 003 (Karnataka), India. 1Department of Environmental Science, Central University of Kerala, Kasaragod - 671 316 (Kerala), India. 2Department of Microbiology and Fermentation Technology, CSIR-Central Food Technological Research Institute, Mysuru - 570 020 (Karnataka), India. Abstract The volatile constituents of dichloromethane extract of wild edible fruit Flacourtia montana J. Graham was analyzed with the aid of GC-MS. 36 compounds were identified, which included alcohols, esters, aldehydes, ketones, furans and nitrogen compounds. The most predominant volatile organic compounds detected were alcohols followed by alkanes, alkenes and esters. Results revealed that the fruit possessed a fruity, citrus like odor with a fatty flavor. Key words : Flacourtia montana, volatile constituents, wild fruit, aroma, flavor. Introduction Flacourtia montana is an wild fruit found across Western Ghats in India. The fruit is red globose berry which is sweet to taste and astringent in flavor. Profiling of volatile constituents is necessary to ascertain aroma and flavor of fruits. Wide array of volatile compounds are found in fruits which include alcohols, esters, ketones and aldehydes (Wilson et al., 1985). The occurrence of either individual or multiple constituents influences the characteristic flavor of a fruit. Several studies have highlighted the prominence of volatile constituents and their significance (Franco and Janzantii, 2005). Moreover, several biological activities have been attributed to volatile constituents, which find potential applications in food and cosmetics industries. Generally, the volatile profile often differs from fruit to fruit and extraction methods employed (Charles et al., 2000). Hence, assessment of volatile constituents provides a deeper insight in determining the aroma and flavor

title: 3.4.5.EVS.064.pdf
text: profile of fruit and fruit based products (Sagrero-Nieves and Pooter, 1992; Santos et al., 1998). However, till date, no reports exist on volatile constituents of fresh or processed F. montana fruits. Hence, the present study for the first time reports volatile constituents of ripened F. montana. Materials and Methods Ripened fruits of F. montana were harvested from the forest area of Uttara Kannada district in Karnataka, India. Seeds were separated and the pulp from the fruits was extracted using an electric grinder (TTK, Prestige, India). The obtained pulp was stored at -20°C until further processed for chemical analysis. Liquid-liquid extraction was carried out using dichloromethane as solvent following the protocol described (Solis-Solis et al., 2007) at 4°C. Further, organic layer was separated and concentrated using rotary evaporator (Ika, Bangalore). Finally, 0.2 µl was injected in gas chromatography-mass spectroscopy (GC-MS). Gas chromatography–mass spectrometric (GC-MS) analysis of volatile constituents were analyzed using GC (Perkin Elmer, USA) coupled with mass spectrometer (turbo mass) using Helium as a carrier gas with a flow rate of 1 ml/min. 0.2 µl of sample extract was injected into a fused silica column coated with poly di methyl siloxane (30.0 m × 320 μm × 0.25 μm). Column temperature was programmed from 50 to 250°C at an incremental of 2°C/min. Injection temperature was maintained at 150°C and the detector temperature was maintained at 260°C. A split ratio of 1:20 and ionization voltage of 70 eV were maintained. INTRODUCTION Ethnobotany has been de昀椀ned as the study of the relationship between man and his ambient vegetation. The word “Ethno” refers to study of people and “Botany” refers to study of plants. In 1874, Powers had used the term “aboriginal botany” which meant a study of the plants which the aboriginals used for medicine,

title: Ethnobotanical_studies_on_Koyna_Valley%2C_Maharashtra.pdf
text: food, textiles, fabrics, ornaments, etc. Ethnobotany was 昀椀rst coined as a term in 1895 by John Harshberger, he described it as the study of the interaction between people, plants and culture. The studies on Ethnobotany are being concentrated particularly in the underdeveloped and developing countries since last three decades. It is because, there are still some ethnic groups and cultures striving to maintain their age-old wisdom and traditions by staying close to the forests and without the knowledge of modern systems. The Indian subcontinent represents one of the greatest emporia of ethnobotanical wealth. Here, many living groups of people are still more or less isolated from the in昀氀uence of the modern world. They continue to live in close association with vital dependence on their ambient vegetation. They provide scientists unparalleled opportunities for profound research. Kirtikar and Basu (1933) have stated, “The ancient Hindus should be given credit for cultivating what is now called Ethnobotany”. In India, the systematic 昀椀eld and related studies in the subject of ethnobotany were steered/ pioneered by Botanical Survey of India (BSI). Dr. E.K. Janaki Ammal from BSI sometime in mid 昀椀fties studied subsistence food plants of certain tribes of south India and found better prospects of Dioscorea. From 1960, Dr. S.K. Jain, from BSI also started intensive 昀椀eld studies among the tribals of central India. His observations on newer plant resources and intimate relationship of the tribals with their plant environment encouraged him to do similar work in eastern India. According to Jain (1991), the traditional knowledge of plants or the science of Ethnobotany deals with total direct relationship between man and plants. Ethnobotany includes study of food, 昀椀bres, dyes, and tannins, other useful and harmful plants, taboos, avoidances and even magico-religious beliefs about plants (Jain 1967; Ford, 1978). The focus of ethnobotany is now

title: Ethnobotanical_studies_on_Koyna_Valley%2C_Maharashtra.pdf
text: on how plants have been used or are being used, managed and perceived in human societies. Man is dependent on plants from time immemorial. Our knowledge of the intimate relationship between early man and plants has come to us mainly through surviving tradition. This relationship, which now forms the core of the interdisciplinary science. Ethnobotany has thus attracted much more attention not only due to its great academic or historical importance but also due to many economic applications (Jain, 1989). India is recognized as one of the 12 mega-biodiversity centers. It has two biodiversity ‘hotspots’ out of 34 in the world (Mittermeier, 2005). It has also the second largest tribal population in the world after Africa. In Maharashtra, there are 47 scheduled tribal communities with a population of 73.18 lacs, which is 9.27 % of the total population of the state (Kshirsagar, 2000). The constitutional name for the tribals is ‘Anusoochit Janajati’ (Scheduled folk communities). These tribal people mostly live in the forests, hills, plateaus and in naturally isolated regions and depend on forest ETHNOBOTANICAL STUDIES ON KOYNA VALLEY, MAHARASHTRA 3 for their livelihood. Plants and their parts are not only used as food and medicine but are also used in various rituals of their social and religious life. Forest is an integral part of their social, religious and economic life. Ethnobotanical investigations in tribal areas, under All India Coordinated Research Project on Ethnobiology (AICRPE) revealed that, out of 9500 wild plants, 7500 plants are used as medicine, 3900 for edible use, 700 for other material and cultural requirements, 525 for 昀椀bre and cordage, 400 as fodder, 300 as pesticides, 300 as gum, resin and dyes, 100 as incense and

The Koyna region lies at the southern end of the Sahyadri sub clusters and recognized as one of the hotspots among Western Ghats. In 1985, Koyna region is declared as Wildlife Sanctuary covering an area of 423.55 sq. km. (Singh & Singh, 2002). Geographically the region is situated between 73 ° 33′ to 73 ° 51′ E longitudes and 17 ° 21′ to 17 ° 46′ N latitudes. Elevation ranges from 600–1100 m (Min. Environment & Forests, 2006). The Koyna region comes under Taluka Patan of Satara district in Maharashtra State. An only river ‘Koyna’ 昀氀ows from the area where a largest dam in Western Ghats was constructed on Koyna reservoir in 1962 mainly for hydroelectric purposes. Geology: Geologically there is an immense accumulation of volcanic rocks, principally basaltic lavas, and known as Deccan trap. The word trap is applied to the step like aspect of the weathered hills of basalt which is the most common feature in the Koyna valley. Perhaps due to basaltic lava, the area is centre of massive earthquake measuring 7.5 on the Richter Scale in December 11, 1967. As the soils of Koyna region are formed from Deccan traps it is generally from the augite or amygdaloidal basalt. These soils are black, dark brown or reddish in colour and hence called Black cotton soil or Regur meaning red soil. Climate: Climate in the Koyna region is monsoonal. Rainfall and humidity in Konkan and Sahydris equable and suitable for plant growth. There is no extreme of hot or cold. Generally from the last week of March to 1st week of May, it is very pleasant. The highest rainfall recorded in the area is 5000 mm. The mean rainfall in the area is 2500 mm.

text: The temperature in the Koyna region and whole state vary from 10 ° to 42.7 ° C. The humidity in Koyna and all through Maharashtra is low. Average mean humidity ranges between 56% to 74%. The relative mean humidity is as high as 80% in July–August but the lowest in March–April. Vegetation: According to Champion and Seth (1968), the forest types seen in the area are southern tropical evergreen forests and southern moist mixed deciduous forests. The vegetation is observed in three di昀昀erent zonations. Top layer: Bombax ceiba is the chief deciduous species associated with Dalbergia latifolia, Terminalia paniculata, Tectona grandis etc. Middle layer : This consists Careya arborea, Erythrina indica, Grewia tiliifolia etc. Ground layer: The undergrowth consists of Carissa congesta, Helicteres isora, Holarrhena antidysenterica, Wrightia tinctoria etc. BOTANICAL SURVEY OF INDIA4 Tribals: Traditionally this area has been inhabited by two communities Kunabis & Dhanagar Gavalies. Only few families are neo-Buddhists. The Kunabies (also called as Maratha) are the main agriculturist community in the Maharashtra where as the Gavali Dhanagars belong to Dhanagar caste cluster who are shepherds & cowherds. The main crops cultivated by them in the area are Ragi (Eleusine coracana (L.) Gaertn.), Rice (Oryza sativa L.) & Vari (Panicum miliaceum L.). Some pulses, oilseeds & other crops are also grown at convenient locations. However the productivity is very low. The villages and hamlets are situated far away in the remote inaccessible areas of hilly region and devoid of modern facilities. The communities here are still following their primitive pattern of life which they have inherited from their ancestors. Their knowledge about basic needs like food, shelter and health-medicine are ful昀椀lled by the surrounding biodiversity. These are still new to urban society and modern scienti昀椀c workers of today. FOOD PLANTS During discussions with women for various edible plants in the form of fruits, vegetables etc. cooked vegetables from leaves of Celosia argentea (Kuradu), Clerodendrum serratum (Bharabgi), Dioscorea pentaphylla (Shendavel) Hygrophila schulli (Kate kolisna) etc. were tasted and found to be delicious. The value of the fruits of Embelia drupacea (Vashingi) was also experienced during thirst and hunger while collection. Most of the wild edible plants observed have high nutritive value. e.g. Meyna laxi昀氀ora (Alu) is known to contain proteins. But it is unknown to these people. Few workers like Gopalan & al. (1977), Nilgaonkar & al. (1985), Ghate & al. (1988), Vaidya & al. (2004), Vartak and Ghate (2004) have made e昀昀orts for analysis of few edible plants. However the other valuable edible plants should be chemically analysed, nutritionally studied for their actual mode of action on the human system and harmful e昀昀ects, if any. (Vartak, 1980). If this data is made available to the modern researchers then they will go in search of these wild edible plants. Nowadays modern people are in touch with the costly and chemically polluted food. Therefore, awareness regarding the nutritive value of these wild edibles is needed. If they will include some of these materials in the diet, it will save their expenditure. It also helps the conservation of traditional knowledge, life & culture before its extinction through the aggressive modern civilization. Out of the 13 Dicot families, Moraceae predominates with 3 plants, Combretaceae and Myrtaceae with 2 plants and other 10 families with 1 plant each. text: 1962, a dam is constructed on the Koyna River which is one of the largest dams in the Western Ghats. However, unlike other dams it has been constructed mainly for hydro-electric purposes. Due to the construction of dam, 98 villages submerged in the Koyna valley from Mahabaleshwar to the dam site at Koynanagar (about 86 km.). For conservation of Medicinal Plants in Koyna region following methodology is adopted by self through NGO Shramjivi Janata Sahayyak Mandal, Rammala (Koyna) (Plate XV). Documentation: The medicinal plants in the form of herbarium sheets, slides & the manual and the knowledge of 60 traditional practitioners (Vaidu) are documented at Rammala (Koyna). Organization of awareness camps & village programmes: For awareness regarding conservation, cultivation, propagation and use of medicinal plants & traditional knowledge the camps and exhibitions of medicinal plants were organized at Rammala (Koyna) as well as in the meetings of community based organizations. The women as village health workers (VHWs) were selected and trained and supplied with herbal 昀椀rst-aid kits for providing health service at village level. The villagers were provided with trainings and seedlings for promotion and establishment of kitchen herbal gardens (KHGs) at village level. Ex-situ conservation: The major facilities for ex-situ conservation are botanical gardens, 昀椀eld gene banks, cryobanks, tissue culture, repositories etc. In India, there are 150 organized botanic gardens, of which Central or State Governments manage 33 gardens; 70 gardens are in public domains and 40 gardens run by Universities (Chakraverty & Mukhopadhyay, 1990). In present study for ex-situ conservation, the activities like Seed collection, nursery preparation and establishment of demonstrative garden at Rammala (Koyna) are carried out. Along with this, a few endemic and medicinal plants e.g. Cajanus lineatus, Moullava spicata introduced in botanical garden of BSI, WC, Pune and some medicinal plants like Acorus calamus, Abrus precatorius, Bacopa monnieri, Centella asiatica, Cymbopogon citratus, Spilanthus calva etc. are introduced

Enterprise development (Co-operative Herbal Processing unit): The raw material in the form of fruits, 昀氀owers, leaves, roots etc. is collected through the trained Women Self Help Groups (SHG), traditional practitioners and Co-operative members.
